title: Tie the camel, then trust
hookLine: no soul dies until its provision is complete (Ibn Majah)
carry: rizq is written: tie the camel, then trust
tomorrow: dad and Amira snap over the dishes. what did the Prophet do at home?

lines: YOUR RIZQ IS WRITTEN. WHY TRY?
NO SOUL DIES BEFORE ITS PROVISION.
cards: An envelope on the kitchen counter, opened, then folded back up. A financial aid letter, with a gap where the number should have been bigger. Somebody at home says the old line: your rizq is written.
Your provision. So if it's written, why try at all? The question is old, and so is the line.
It comes from a hadith in Sunan Ibn Majah: no soul will die until it has received its provision in full.

teach.b: Hear the whole report first. The Prophet ﷺ said: fear God and be gentle in seeking. No soul dies until it has its full provision, even if it comes slowly.
So take what is lawful and leave what is forbidden. The Qur'an says it of every creature. In Pickthall's words: "And there is not a beast in the earth but the sustenance thereof dependeth on Allah."
Now two readings, both inside the tradition. The first leans on trust.
Another hadith says that if you relied on God as you truly should, He would provide for you as He provides for the birds: they go out hungry in the morning and come back full.
Some readers hear that and say: loosen your grip. The scramble itself is the problem. The second leans on effort.
A man asked the Prophet: should I tie my camel and trust God, or leave her loose and trust?
Tie her, he said, and trust. Effort isn't a lack of faith; it's part of it. And look again at the birds.
They don't wait in the nest. They go out.
Both readings agree on the thing to drop: the panic.
Written doesn't mean stop applying. It means the worry gets smaller than the work. One for tonight: in the hadith of the birds, the trusting ones are the ones who leave home early.

how: Muslims speak of rizq, provision, as coming from God, and pair tawakkul, trust, with effort, as in the hadith 'tie her, and trust'; some say hasbiyallah when money worries press.

o: people born rich were destined to stay rich
what you're given to live on is already measured
money saved now is guaranteed to you later

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: no soul dies before its provision
go out hungry, come back full
every creature's sustenance is on God

s: if provision is written, Islam says there's no point working for it
tie her, and trust: effort is part of trust, not a lack of it.
in the hadith, the birds go out hungry and come back full
they trust, and they still leave the nest.
the Ibn Majah report says to be gentle in seeking
no soul dies before its full provision, so seek it without panic.

games.q: your cousin says the birds hadith means she can stop job hunting and just trust. before you answer, what's the best case for her side?
o: relying on God truly is what provides, so the frantic scramble is the real problem.
the hadith says the birds stay in the nest and the food comes to them.
the Qur'an says effort shows weak faith, so job hunting is a mistake.
games.why: her best case is the trust half: rely on God truly, and drop the panic. the other side adds: the birds still go out, and the camel still gets tied.

practice: Name one money worry in a few words, in your head or on paper. Then name one thing that's yours to do this week, the tied camel, and one thing that isn't, the part you hand over.
Some Muslims say hasbiyallah, God is enough for me, as they set that second part down.

wordCard.voice: Provision is written: your rizq, what you're given to live on, is already measured. You still go out to seek it, gently.

orig.note: Arabic: provision, sustenance; whatever God gives a soul to live on.

carryVoice: Pocket this: rizq is written, so tie the camel, then trust. That's ten of ten for work and money.
